title: Few executions
hookLine: he is remembered for rarely using the death penalty

lines: THE POWER TO END A LIFE.
THE ROPE AND THE SWORD AT HAND.
cards: A ruler in that age held the power to end a life with a word: a thief, a rebel, a man who tried to kill the king himself. The rope and the sword were close at hand. So it's striking what Ranjit Singh is remembered for.
Not the size of his army this time, or the gold on the Harmandir, but how seldom he gave the order.

teach.b: Histories of his reign, including the accounts of foreign visitors, say the Maharaja rarely used the death penalty, even for serious crimes.
Punishment came instead as fines or loss of office, and sometimes as harsh bodily punishment, which belongs in the honest picture too. But the gallows were not his habit.

Tradition tells of people who attacked or plotted against him and were spared. Whatever the details, the memory is consistent: this was a ruler who would rather keep a man alive. Why does that matter for a Sikh king?
The Gurus taught that the one Lord is in every heart.

teach.h: WHERE FORGIVENESS IS, THE LORD IS.
teach.b: And among the saloks of Kabir in the Guru Granth Sahib is a short run of pairs: where there is spiritual wisdom, there is righteousness; where there is falsehood, there is sin; where there is greed, there is death; and where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord himself.
A ruler who took that seriously would think twice before ending a life.

teach.h: MERCY FROM ONE WHO COULD DO OTHERWISE.
teach.b: And mercy is not weakness. Ranjit Singh was no soft ruler. He fought hard, took cities, and kept a tight hold on his kingdom.
That's what makes the memory interesting: he had every means to kill, and chose, again and again, not to.
Mercy means the most in the hands of someone who could do otherwise.

how: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh's rare use of the death penalty as part of his legacy, and connect it with the teaching in the Guru Granth Sahib that where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord.

o: a vow to stop fighting wars and battles for good
rarely ordering death, though he had the power
a law that banned all punishment in the kingdom

games.q: mercy in power — tap the pairs.
p: there is death, in Kabir's salok

s: the Maharaja is remembered for rarely ordering death
histories of his reign, including foreign visitors, say so.
his kingdom had no harsh punishments at all
fines and loss of office were common, and some punishments were harsh.
his mercy came from a weak hold on power
he fought hard and held his kingdom tightly; that's what makes the mercy striking.

games.q: you're the Maharaja. a man has tried to harm you. the court expects a death sentence. what is he remembered for doing, more often than not?
games.why: tradition tells of people who acted against him and were spared; he's remembered for rarely ordering death.

practice: Think of one place where you hold a little power, over a child, a coworker, a sibling, or yourself, and bring to mind someone there who has let you down.
Without excusing anything, picture choosing mercy instead, just once, and notice how it feels to hold the power and not use it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Few executions. The Maharaja who held the power of life and death, and is remembered for how rarely he used it.

orig.note: khima, forgiveness; Kabir's salok says that where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord himself.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy in power. Where there is forgiveness, Kabir says, there is the Lord. That's day nine hundred twenty-one.

sources.work: J. D. Cunningham, A History of the Sikhs
